title: What a rocket launch's sound does to your ears 🚀
subject: rocket
description:
How close would you dare to stand? 👇

How loud is a rocket launch, and what does that sound do to your body? Microphones at NASA's Artemis I launch measured chainsaw-level noise 3 miles away, and the Saturn V reached about 203 decibels.

Sources: Smithsonian Magazine, "How Loud Was NASA's Artemis 1 Launch?" (BYU study, JASA Express Letters; CDC hearing thresholds); BYU Physics, "Debunking acoustics myths around the Saturn V" (Kent Gee, 2022); Space.com, "No, NASA's massive Saturn V rocket didn't melt concrete with sound"; NASA, "Pad 39B Water Flow Test Comes Through Loud and Clear" (2019).

scenes.text: Stand 3 miles from this rocket, and your ears hurt.
At NASA's Artemis I launch in 2022, BYU microphones 3 miles away recorded 129 decibels. That's a chainsaw.
At 1 mile, 136. Ear pain starts around 120.
The Saturn V hit about 203. Physicist Kent Gee says 200 is like 10,000 jet engines.
That can rupture an eardrum. Apollo crowds were kept 3.5 miles back.
Now NASA floods the pad with 450,000 gallons of water. It's not for fire. It knocks the sound down.
